title: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control
summary: Describes how QUIC detects lost packets and controls congestion. It covers the timers and acknowledgment-based logic used to decide that data needs to be resent, and a congestion controller that keeps senders from overloading the network.

eli5.summary: QUIC has to notice when a packet is lost and slow down when the road is crowded. This explains how it does both.

questions: how does quic detect packet loss
what is a quic probe timeout
what is persistent congestion in quic
how is quic congestion control different from tcp
subtitle: How a QUIC sender decides a packet is lost, when to send probes, and how fast it may send.

tldr.problem: A transport protocol has to notice when packets are lost and back off when the network is overloaded. QUIC differs from TCP in ways that change how this works.
tldr.mechanism: QUIC senders measure round-trip time, declare packets lost from acknowledgments (a packet threshold and a time threshold), use a probe timeout to recover from tail loss, and run a NewReno-style congestion controller with slow start, recovery and congestion avoidance.
tldr.outcome: The result is a complete sender-side recovery design for QUIC. Senders may swap in a different congestion controller, as long as it follows the guidelines of RFC 8085.

facts.label: Initial window
facts.value: 10 x max datagram size, capped at larger of 14,720 bytes or 2 x max datagram size

today: RFC 9002 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2021, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata. It works together with RFC 9000 and RFC 9001.

sections.title: Scope and Packet Basics
sections.content:
RFC 9002 describes the loss detection and congestion control mechanisms for QUIC, a secure, general-purpose transport protocol defined in RFC 9000.

Every QUIC packet carries a packet number. Packet numbers never repeat within a packet number space for the lifetime of a connection, and they increase monotonically. When data is declared lost, it goes into a new packet with a new number, so the sender never has to guess whether an acknowledgment refers to the original or the retransmission.

Three terms matter throughout. Ack-eliciting frames are all frames other than ACK, PADDING and CONNECTION_CLOSE. Ack-eliciting packets contain at least one of them. In-flight packets are ack-eliciting or contain PADDING, and have been sent but not yet acknowledged, declared lost or discarded along with old keys.
sections.eli5: Every note gets a bigger number than the last one, and a lost note is rewritten with a brand new number. That way nobody gets confused about which note was answered.

sections.title: How QUIC Differs from TCP
sections.content:
The algorithms here parallel well-known TCP ones, but protocol differences change them. The RFC lists these differences.

  • Separate packet number spaces for each encryption level (0-RTT and all generations of 1-RTT keys share one space). Congestion control and RTT measurement are unified across spaces.
  • Transmission order is separate from delivery order. Packet numbers show send order, and stream offsets show delivery order. This removes TCP's retransmission ambiguity.
  • Clearer loss epoch. A loss epoch starts when a packet is lost and ends when any packet sent after it is acknowledged, so the window shrinks once per round trip that sees loss.
  • No reneging. A packet acknowledgment cannot be taken back, which simplifies both sides.
  • More ACK ranges than TCP's three SACK ranges, which speeds recovery in high-loss environments.
  • Explicit acknowledgment delay. Endpoints report how long they held an acknowledgment, which sharpens the peer's RTT estimate.

The probe timeout (PTO) replaces TCP's RTO and tail loss probe. The recommended minimum congestion window is two packets instead of one. Lost handshake packets are treated like any other loss, not as persistent congestion.
sections.eli5: QUIC fixes some old TCP headaches: each note has its own number, you can say which notes arrived in more detail, and you tell your friend how long you waited before answering.

sections.title: Estimating Round-Trip Time
sections.content:
For each path an endpoint keeps three values: min_rtt (the minimum observed over a period), smoothed_rtt (an exponentially weighted moving average) and rttvar (the mean deviation).

A sample, latest_rtt, is the time from sending the largest acknowledged packet to receiving its acknowledgment. A sample is taken only when that largest packet is newly acknowledged and at least one newly acknowledged packet was ack-eliciting. An RTT sample MUST NOT be generated otherwise, because an ACK for only non-ack-eliciting packets could carry an arbitrarily large delay.

The first sample sets smoothed_rtt to the sample and rttvar to half of it. Later samples are adjusted for the peer's reported acknowledgment delay, which is capped at the peer's max_ack_delay once the handshake is confirmed, and are never reduced below min_rtt. Then smoothed_rtt = 7/8 * smoothed_rtt + 1/8 * adjusted_rtt and rttvar = 3/4 * rttvar + 1/4 * |smoothed_rtt - adjusted_rtt|.

The min_rtt uses only locally observed times, so a peer that misreports delay cannot push it down.
sections.eli5: To guess how long a note takes to travel, you time a few trips and keep a running average, mostly trusting your past average and a little bit the newest trip.

sections.title: Declaring Packets Lost
sections.content:
A packet is declared lost when it is unacknowledged, in flight, and was sent before an acknowledged packet, and either it was sent kPacketThreshold packets before that acknowledged packet or it was sent long enough ago. Both tests tolerate some reordering.

  • Packet threshold: the recommended initial value is 3, and implementations SHOULD NOT use less than 3, to stay similar to TCP.
  • Time threshold: max(kTimeThreshold * max(smoothed_rtt, latest_rtt), kGranularity). The recommended kTimeThreshold is 9/8 of an RTT and the recommended kGranularity is 1 millisecond.

Loss detection is kept separate for each packet number space, unlike RTT measurement and congestion control, because loss detection also depends on key availability. Spurious loss declarations cause needless retransmissions, so implementations can raise the thresholds when they detect them.

Special cases cover a Retry packet (the client resets congestion control and loss recovery state) and discarded keys (when Initial or Handshake keys are dropped, the sender MUST discard the recovery state for those packets and remove them from bytes in flight).
sections.eli5: If a note you sent earlier never got answered but a note you sent later did, or if too much time passed, you decide the first one was probably lost.

sections.title: The Probe Timeout
sections.content:
Acknowledgment-based detection cannot help when nothing more arrives, such as when the last packets are lost. For that the sender arms a probe timeout (PTO). When it fires, the sender sends one or two probe datagrams. A PTO expiry does not mean packets were lost and MUST NOT cause unacknowledged packets to be marked lost.

The period is PTO = smoothed_rtt + max(4*rttvar, kGranularity) + max_ack_delay, computed per packet number space. For Initial and Handshake spaces, max_ack_delay is taken as 0. Each time the PTO fires, the backoff doubles the period, and it is reset when an acknowledgment arrives (a client does not reset it on Initial acknowledgments while the server may still be validating its address).

When no earlier RTT is available, the initial RTT SHOULD be 333 milliseconds, giving a first PTO of 1 second like TCP's initial RTO. All probe packets MUST be ack-eliciting, and an endpoint MAY send up to two full-sized datagrams. If there is nothing to send, the sender SHOULD send a PING or other ack-eliciting frame.

Until the server has validated the client's address it can send only three times the data it received, so the server's PTO is not armed when it has nothing it may send, and the client must keep sending packets to unblock it.
sections.eli5: If you hear nothing back for a while, you poke your friend with a small message to check, and each time you wait twice as long before poking again.

sections.title: Congestion Control States
sections.content:
The RFC specifies a sender-side controller similar to TCP NewReno. Other algorithms, such as CUBIC, may be used by a sender on its own, but then the controller MUST follow Section 3.1 of RFC 8085. The controller works per path, in bytes, and an endpoint MUST NOT send if it would push bytes in flight above the congestion window, except for PTO probes and when entering recovery.

  • Slow start: the window grows by the bytes acknowledged, which is exponential growth. The slow start threshold begins at infinity. The sender leaves on a lost packet or an increase in the peer's ECN-CE count.
  • Recovery: the slow start threshold is set to half the window, and the window is reduced to it. It aims for one reduction per round trip. Recovery ends when a packet sent during it is acknowledged.
  • Congestion avoidance: additive increase, multiplicative decrease. The window may grow at most one maximum datagram size per window acknowledged.

The initial window SHOULD be ten times the maximum datagram size, limited to the larger of 14,720 bytes or twice the maximum datagram size. The recommended minimum window is 2 * max_datagram_size.
sections.eli5: You start by sending a few notes and doubling quickly. When one goes missing, you cut back by half, then creep up slowly so you do not clog the hallway.

sections.title: Persistent Congestion and Pacing
sections.content:
If a sender loses everything it sent over a long enough stretch, the network is treated as being in persistent congestion. This is established when two ack-eliciting packets are declared lost, no packet sent between them was acknowledged, the time between them exceeds the persistent congestion duration, and a prior RTT sample existed. The duration is (smoothed_rtt + max(4*rttvar, kGranularity) + max_ack_delay) * kPersistentCongestionThreshold, with a recommended threshold of 3. The window then drops to the minimum window.

The RFC walks through an example with a period of 2 and a threshold of 3: the lost packets span 7 time units, which exceeds the duration of 6, so persistent congestion is declared.

Pacing: a sender SHOULD pace its in-flight packets, and MUST either pace or limit bursts, which SHOULD be limited to the initial window. Packets containing only ACK frames SHOULD NOT be paced. When the window is underutilized, because the application has no data or flow control blocks it, it SHOULD NOT be increased.
sections.eli5: If a long run of your notes all vanish, you assume the hallway is really jammed and drop back to sending only a couple at a time. You also space notes out instead of throwing a pile at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Loss detection and congestion control consume signals such as delay, loss and ECN markings from unauthenticated entities. An attacker can make endpoints slow down by dropping packets, altering path delay or changing ECN codepoints.

Packets that carry only ACK frames can be spotted by size, and acknowledgment patterns can reveal link or application behavior. Endpoints can bundle acknowledgments with other frames or use PADDING, at a possible cost to performance.

A receiver can misreport ECN markings. Hiding ECN-CE reports could make a sender speed up, and a sender can detect this by occasionally marking its own packets ECN-CE, then disabling ECN on that path if the mark is not reported back. Reporting extra ECN-CE markings only slows the sender, so no advantage is gained.
sections.eli5: Because the signals come from the open network, a troublemaker could trick a sender into slowing down or speeding up. QUIC has a few tricks to spot the cheating and to hide patterns.
